title: The Smiling Winter
premise: Orsen Delacroix, a hospice nurse who has heard the dying count backwards for seven years, returns to their late grandmother's house and discovers every family photograph now contains an empty wooden chair that wasn't there before. The chair belongs to the Founder, a presence the town of Hollowmere bound generations ago through a ritual that requires a willing heir every sixty years—and the deadline is the winter solstice, nine days away. As Orsen uncovers their grandmother's hidden role as the last Keeper, the town's warm, suffocating welcome curdles into something hungry, and the dying begin counting toward Orsen instead of zero. In the end, Orsen must choose between completing the ritual and becoming the Founder's new vessel, or breaking it and letting the thing they've spent a lifetime hiding from finally see them—choosing found family over the town's false one, at the cost of the house, the town's memory of them, and nearly their own name.
about_author: R. M. Coldharbour is the pen name of a former night-shift caregiver who spent a decade in palliative wards across the northern Midwest, where the silence between rounds was often louder than the machines. They write horror about the tenderness that curdles when small towns decide you belong to them.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. After their grandmother's funeral, Orsen returns to the house to pack it up and notices every family photograph now includes a plain wooden chair no one remembers—positioned closer to the camera in each successive decade. The emotional beat is dread wrapped in grief: Orsen, who has spent seven years rationalizing the backwards counting they hear at the hospice, cannot rationalize the chair. Ends with Orsen finding the chair itself in the locked attic, still warm.

chapters.title: Counting Backwards
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Back at the hospice, a dying patient grabs Orsen's wrist and counts down from sixty instead of ten, whispering 'nine days' at zero. Another patient across the ward opens her eyes and says, in unison, 'nine days.' Orsen realizes the counting has never been random—it's a clock. The emotional beat is the collapse of Orsen's lifelong coping strategy: explanations are running out faster than time.

chapters.title: Hollowmere Welcomes You Home
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV, with interludes of neighbor Mrs. Vane's diary. Orsen returns to Hollowmere, where the town greets them with unsettling warmth—casseroles, offers to help, everyone already knowing their name. Mrs. Vane's old diary entries, slipped into Orsen's mailbox, describe a 'Founding Supper' and warn: 'They smile so you won't count the chairs at the table.' The emotional beat is belonging that feels like a trap closing.

chapters.title: What Grandma Kept
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Searching the attic, Orsen finds their grandmother's Keeper journal: the town's founders bound a presence they called the Guest to protect Hollowmere's first winter, and every sixty years an heir must sit in the chair and 'hold the door' or the Guest walks free. Orsen learns their grandmother spent decades preparing them—every childhood visit, every story—was grooming. The emotional beat is betrayal braided with reluctant understanding.

chapters.title: The Photographs Move
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. The photographs change again: the chair is no longer empty. A blurred figure sits in it, and in each photo it is slightly more defined, slightly closer to the family members—now including Orsen in the most recent picture, which was taken the day they arrived. The hospice calls: the counting patients have stopped counting. The emotional beat is the horror of being watched by something that considers itself family.

chapters.title: Nine Chairs at the Supper
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Orsen and town patriarch Aldous Merrick. Aldous invites Orsen to the Founders' Hall and reveals the town knows the deadline; he frames the ritual as sacrifice, as love, as the reason Hollowmere has never known famine or cold deaths. Orsen sees the founding portraits: eight founders, nine chairs. Aldous admits the ninth chair has always waited for 'the one who hears.' The emotional beat is seduction—the genuine temptation of belonging.

chapters.title: The Ones Who Refused
chapters.summary: Mrs. Vane's POV, framed as her final diary entries read by Orsen. Vane reveals her sister was the heir sixty years ago and refused; the town didn't punish her—they simply stopped perceiving her, erased her from every photograph and memory, and the Guest took 'a little of everyone' instead. Vane, half-erased herself, begs Orsen to run before the solstice. The emotional beat is grief for the erased and terror of a fate worse than death: being unremembered.

chapters.title: Solstice Eve
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Orsen packs to flee, but the roads out of Hollowmere loop back to the house no matter which direction they drive; the hospice patients' voices now come from the attic, counting from nine. The Guest speaks through the photographs for the first time, gentle and patient: 'You were never invisible to me. You were mine.' The emotional beat is the shattering of Orsen's last illusion—that hiding was ever an option.

chapters.title: The Sitting
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV, climax. On the solstice night, the town gathers at the house, smiling, to witness the ritual. Orsen sits in the chair as instructed—but instead of opening the door, they use the Keeper's bond to speak to the Guest directly, offering it what no founder ever did: acknowledgment instead of imprisonment. The Guest, revealed as something that only ever wanted to be counted, begins to unbind itself—and Hollowmere begins to scream. The emotional beat is courage: choosing truth over the comfort of the lie.

chapters.title: What the Winter Remembers
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV, resolution. The ritual breaks; the house burns; the Guest departs with the first thaw wind, and the town forgets Orsen entirely—except for a handful of the dying, who smile and count forwards now, one to ten, and let go in peace. Orsen leaves Hollowmere carrying only one photograph: the family, the empty ninth chair, and themselves, remembered by no one but the reader. The emotional beat is bittersweet freedom—Orsen finally belongs to themselves.
